Aim Acanthosis nigricans (AN) is a strong correlate of obesity and is considered a marker of insulin resistance (IR). AN is associated with various other cardiometabolic risk factors (CMRFs). However, the direct causal relationship of IR with AN in obesity has been debated. Therefore, we aimed to examine the complex causal relationships among the troika of AN, obesity, and IR in Mexican Americans (MAs). Methods We used data from 670 non-diabetic MA children, aged 6–17 years (49% girls). AN (prevalence 33%) severity scores (range 0–5) were used as a quasi-quantitative trait (AN-q) for analysis. We used the program SOLAR for determining phenotypic, genetic, and environmental correlations between AN-q and CMRFs (e.g., BMI, HOMA-IR, lipids, blood pressure, hs-C-reactive protein (CRP), and Harvard physical fitness score (PFS)). The genetic and environmental correlations were subsequently used in mediation analysis (AMOS program). Model comparisons were made using goodness-of-fit indexes. Results Heritability of AN-q was 0.75 (p<0.0001). It was positively/significantly (p<0.05) correlated with traits such as BMI, HOMA-IR, and CRP, and negatively with HDL-C and PFS. Of the models tested, indirect mediation analysis of BMI→HOMA-IR→AN-q yielded lower goodness-of-fit than a partial mediation model where BMI explained the relationship with both HOMA-IR and AN-q simultaneously. Using complex models, BMI was associated with AN-q and IR mediating most of the CMRFs; but no relationship between IR and AN-q. Introduction Acanthosis nigricans (AN) is an epidermal disorder of velvety thickening that primarily affects the axillae, posterior neck fold, flexor skin surfaces, and umbilicus [ 1 , 2 ]. AN has been associated with obesity and insulin resistance (IR) [ 1 , 2 ]; and, has been used as a marker for assessing type 2 diabetes (T2DM) risk in children [ 3 ]. For example, individuals with body mass index (BMI) greater than the 98 th percentile were found to have a 62% prevalence of AN [ 4 ]; and, the presence of AN in Mexican individuals could predict IR with 66.7% sensitivity, which was shown to be influenced by the skin phototype [ 5 ]. Thus, AN has been used as a screening tool for identifying children at risk of insulin resistance (IR), T2DM, and cardiometabolic risk factors (CMRF) [ 2 , 6 – 8 ], in order to prevent progression of these disease conditions into adulthood. There are remarkable ethnic disparities in the prevalence of AN. For example, in the United States (US), according to a cross-sectional study of young persons (the Research in Outpatient Settings Network), the prevalence of AN was found to be higher in Hispanics (19%) and American Indians (28%) compared to non-Hispanic whites (3%) [ 9 ]. As we reported previously, the occurrence of AN in Mexican Americans (MA) children and adolescents from families at high risk for obesity, CMRFs, and T2DM was 33% [ 10 ]. The diversity in clinical manifestations of AN can be attributed to the influences of genetic and environmental factors and their interactive influences on AN. Aside from these observations, it is not known whether AN and its clinical correlates, particularly obesity and IR, are causally related. Recently, Hudson et al. [ 11 ], using data from a community sample of adolescents with obesity, found that AN (or severity) was a poor marker of IR or cardiometabolic risk after adjusting for obesity (i.e., BMI). Therefore, since the direct causal relationship of IR with AN in obesity is debatable, we aimed to assess genetic and environmental correlations between AN and CMRFs and examine the complex causal relationships among the troika of AN, obesity, and IR using data from children and adolescents from MA families. In contrast to population studies comprising of unrelated individuals, family-based studies such as ours provide opportunities not only to determine genetic basis of given traits, but also to assess phenotypic, genetic, and environmental correlations among correlated traits such as IR, AN, and obesity. Here, we analyzed the association of AN severity score with IR, obesity measures and other CMRFs. To assess the effects of IR and obesity on AN and other CMRFs, a mediation model was employed using information from the matrices of genetic and environmental correlations.

extracted_data.document_summary: This study investigated the complex causal relationships and genetic basis among Acanthosis nigricans (AN), obesity (BMI), and insulin resistance (IR) in a cohort of 670 non-diabetic Mexican American children (aged 6-17 years) from 401 nuclear families. Using variance components and mediation analysis, the research aimed to determine how AN correlates with various cardiometabolic risk factors (CMRFs) and whether IR or obesity primarily drives the association. The key finding is that obesity largely explains the observed association between IR and AN, with no direct causal relationship found between IR and AN when obesity is accounted for, highlighting AN's utility as a non-invasive clinical marker for obesity-driven cardiometabolic risk and its ability to predict future Type 2 Diabetes risk.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Observational study investigating cardiometabolic risk factors and a diagnostic marker
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This was an observational study with no therapeutic intervention or dose administered. Data was collected from 670 non-diabetic Mexican American children aged 6–17 years from a family-based cohort, focusing on associations and the utility of Acanthosis Nigricans as a screening tool for cardiometabolic risk factors, including extensive clinical tests and interviews on medical history, demographic, phenotypic, and environmental variables.

analyzed_biomarkers.activity_type: Clinical visual assessment / severity score (quasi-quantitative trait)

measured_effect.direction_of_change: correlated (positive with BMI, HOMA-IR, CRP, WC; negative with HDL-C, PFS); higher prevalence with obesity/prediabetes/MS
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Heritability of AN-q was 0.75 (p<0.0001); h² for AN severity score was 0.75 ± 0.11 (P < 3.6 x 10⁻¹²). Positively/significantly correlated with BMI, HOMA-IR, and CRP (p<0.05). Negatively correlated with HDL-C and PFS (p<0.05). Prevalence 33% in the study population. Severity scores range 0–5. Occurrence of AN increased by obesity status: normal weight (11%), overweight (53%), and obese (65%); by prediabetes status (47%); and by MS status (67%). Children with AN are approximately 9/10 times more likely to be obese/overweight, 6 times more likely to have MS, and 2 times more likely to have prediabetes. Phenotypic correlations (ρP) with CMRFs ranged from -0.35 (with PFS) to 0.66 (with WC). Genetic correlations (ρG) ranged from -0.57 (with PFS) to 0.79 (with WC). Obesity is a direct contributor to AN, which itself is a compound marker of complex cardiometabolic risk.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Epidermal disorder associated with metabolic dysfunction; considered a marker of insulin resistance and obesity. Its pathogenesis may involve activation of insulin-like growth factor-1 receptors or fibroblast growth factor receptors by excess insulin.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Observational study in non-diabetic Mexican American children, examining causal relationships between AN, obesity, and insulin resistance; association with obesity, prediabetes, metabolic syndrome (MS), and cardiometabolic risk factors (CMRFs).
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Strong correlate of obesity and a marker of insulin resistance, associated with various cardiometabolic risk factors. It is a compound marker of metabolic risk and a valuable, simple non-invasive clinical tool for pediatric screening of cardiometabolic risks (e.g., Type 2 Diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidemia).

analyzed_biomarkers.measured_tissue_or_fluid: Whole body (derived from anthropometric measurements of height and weight)

measured_effect.direction_of_change: positively correlated; identified as a direct contributor and attenuator of other relationships
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Positively/significantly correlated with AN-q (p<0.05). High rates of overweight (19.1%) and obesity (34%) were found in the study population. AN-q exhibited a linear trend with BMI (ANOVA for linear trend p < 0.001). A partial mediation model where BMI explained the relationship with both HOMA-IR and AN-q simultaneously had a better goodness-of-fit. BMI was associated with AN-q and HOMA-IR, mediating most of the associations with CMRFs. BMI had a partial effect, not only on IR and AN, but also on inflammation, blood pressure, lipids and physical fitness. Obesity (measured by BMI) is a direct contributor to AN, hyperinsulinemia, and other CMRFs; attenuation by BMI is shown for various phenotypic functions (e.g., hsCRP, triglycerides).

analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicator of overweight/obesity; identified as a primary driver of cardiometabolic risk, directly influencing insulin resistance, AN, inflammation, blood pressure, lipids, and physical fitness, with effects often mediating other factors. measured_effect.direction_of_change: positively correlated; effect on AN-q attenuated/non-significant when BMI considered
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Positively/significantly correlated with AN-q (p<0.05). AN-q exhibited a linear trend with HOMA-IR (ANOVA for linear trend p < 0.001). In the partial mediation model, the effect of HOMA-IR on AN-q was completely attenuated/non-significant when BMI was considered, suggesting no direct causal relationship between IR and AN. BMI through IR was found to have remarkable environmental effects on lipid concentrations and physical fitness. HOMA-IR had a minor influence on CRP concentrations.
